content.text:
I submitted **part-based**, with confidence 0.85.

**Design:** I trained the learner on two tasks that share no rules and agree on none of their inputs: L1-S1-M1 and L2-S2-M2. Then I tested two tasks where the hypotheses predict opposite results:
- **L1-S2-M2** uses only rules the learner has already seen, but its mapping is less like the trained tasks (best similarity 0.5).
- **L1-S1-M3** has one new rule, but its mapping is more like a trained task (similarity 0.75).

A part-based learner should find the first one easier. A holistic learner should find the second one easier.

**Results** (examples needed to reach criterion; lower means easier):

| Task | New rules | Best similarity | Tests | Mean |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| L1-S2-M2 | 0 | 0.50 | 14 | 11.4 (median about 5) |
| L1-S1-M3 | 1 | 0.75 | 14 | 21.8 (median about 21) |
| L1-S3-M3 | 2 | 0.56 | 8 | 24.6 |
| L3-S3-M4 | 3 | 0.19 | 6 | 41.7 |

The task built only from known rules was clearly easier, even though its mapping was less similar. Across all four tasks, cost goes up with the number of new rules. It doesn't follow similarity: the most similar task was not the easiest.

The tests were very noisy: single samples ranged from 1 to 61, and the two halves of the key contrast overlap a lot. That's why I kept confidence at 0.85 rather than higher. I used 44 of the 60 budget and left 16 unspent; more repeats of the key contrast would have tightened the estimate a bit.
